extracted.intended_audience: scientists and academics serving as journal peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing effective pre-publication peer reviews of scientific journal manuscripts, covering structure, content, tone, and scope of reviewer comments for editors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contains a brief summary of the entire manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Contains a brief summary of the entire manuscript. Show the editors and authors what you think the main claims of the paper are, and your assessment of its impact on the field. What did the authors try to show and what did they try to claim?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a one-sentence description of the paper’s main point, followed by several sentences summarizing specific important findings that lead to the paper’s logical conclusion. Then, highlight the significance of the important findings and conclude with the reviewer’s overall opinion of what the manuscript does and does not do well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly directs the editor on the path forward (decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly directs the editor on the path forward. Should this paper be accepted, rejected, or revised?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State decision either as part of concluding sentence in the summary or as a separate sentence. Use categories like: Accept with no revisions, Accept with minor revisions, Accept with major revisions, Reject. Note journals may have different wording/options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and locate major concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies any major (internal inconsistencies, missing data, etc.) concerns, and clearly locates them within the document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why you think the direction specified is correct; cite specific page/line numbers or figure references. Major concerns typically lead to reject or accept-with-major-revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: List minor concerns (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists (if appropriate — i.e. if you are suggesting revision or acceptance) minor concerns to help the authors make the paper watertight (typographical errors, grammatical errors, missing references, unclear explanations of methodology, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include minor items such as typographical errors, grammatical errors, missing references, unclear explanations, and figure readability suggestions; these are often included for accept/accept-with-minor-revisions decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how arguments can be better defended
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the arguments can be better defended through analysis, experiments, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where you identify a problem, suggest concrete resolutions (what data/analyses/controls would convince you). Example prompts: what data would be needed to overturn an apparent contradiction with established laws, what additional statistical analyses would be required, or what control experiments are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be reasonable within the original manuscript scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Is reasonable within the original manuscript scope; does not suggest modifications that would require excessive time or expense, or that could instead be addressed by adjusting the manuscript’s claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess feasibility of suggested experiments. Avoid requesting multi-year work or prohibitively expensive experiments; instead suggest adjusting claims to fit evidence if that would render the paper still suitable for the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical review length and high-level structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical peer review is 1-2 pages long. You can divide your content roughly as follows: Identify your purpose; Summary; Decision; Major Concerns; Minor Concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear headings and a consistent order so editors/authors can quickly parse your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scientific integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly explain to the editors and authors any issues that you have identified with the science being reported (within reason), requiring evaluation of scientific integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific integrity issues may require editorial office handling; signal such issues in confidential comments to editors if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate quality of data collection and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate quality of data collection methods and data analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on appropriateness of experimental design, sample sizes, controls, statistical analyses, and whether analyses match the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess veracity of conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the veracity of conclusions presented in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the presented data and analyses support the authors’ conclusions; recommend additional data or claim adjustments if not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine match with journal scope and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine match between the proposed submission and the journal scope (subject matter and potential impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the paper's significance is appropriate for the journal (e.g., a narrow subfield result may be unsuitable for a broad multidisciplinary journal). Consult editor about scope questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze your audience (editor vs. author)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance your review between the two audiences: primary audience is the journal editor; secondary audience is the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember editors want critical feedback on science and guidance on decision; authors want to know what they need to change or add to convince reviewers. Make that distinction in your comments and use confidential comments to editors when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: State your areas of expertise and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the editors your areas of expertise within the manuscript and which aspects you feel qualified to comment on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly which parts of the manuscript you are commenting on (methods, interpretation, statistics, etc.) to help editors weigh your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a standard review format
rubrics_metrics.description: Format your document in a standard way. Most commonly the format is (1) Summary, (2) Decision, (3) Major Concerns, and (4) Minor Concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the journal uses a multiple-choice scoring form, treat it as an additional checklist of topics to address; include the same topics in your free-text review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the summary demonstrate understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary grounds the remainder of your review and demonstrates that you have read and understood the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, concise summary reassures editors that you followed the paper’s logic and helps authors see how others might interpret their claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly state decision and use confidential comments when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Your decision must be clearly stated to aid the interpretation of the rest of your comments. Most reviews also contain the option to provide confidential comments to the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confidential comments for sensitive matters (plagiarism, data manipulation, or serious ethical concerns) and to elaborate on recommendation rationale not appropriate for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major concerns should address significance/novelty/field-specific criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on the journal there might be criteria for significance, novelty, industrial relevance, or other field-specific criteria that need to be accounted for in your major concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about why a major concern affects significance or novelty, and whether it undermines the paper’s suitability for the journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major concerns: internal inconsistency or conflict with field understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Major concerns include issues with the arguments presented in the paper that are not internally consistent, or present arguments that go against significant understanding in the field, without the necessary data to back it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples and explain what data/analyses would be required to reconcile or support such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major concerns: missing key experimental or computational data
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of key experimental or computational data that are vital to justify the claims made in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples (e.g., unexplained GC-MS peaks, claims about human health based only on in vitro data) and specify which experiments/controls/analyses are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite resolutions for major concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most important aspects of providing a review with major concerns is your ability to cite resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State what new data, statistical analyses, or control experiments would convince you that the claims are supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated list of common minor concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor concerns are primarily issues that are raised that would improve the clarity of the message, but don’t impact the logic of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical minor concerns: grammatical errors, typographical errors, missing references, insufficient background or methods information, insufficient or possibly extraneous detail, unclear or poorly worded explanations, incorrect figure labels or readability issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer revisions that are reasonable and in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer revisions that are reasonable and in scope; think about the feasibility of the experiments you suggest to address your concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid requesting work that would be a separate multi-year project; consider whether adjusting claims rather than new experiments would suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure comments for reader usability
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure your comments in a way that makes sense to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate concerns clearly with line breaks or numbering, organize them in the order they appear in the manuscript, quote directly from the text and include page/line/paragraph numbers for easy reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and concision in reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep your comments as brief as possible by simply stating the issue and your suggestion for fixing it in a few sentences or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct, specific phrasing; avoid long digressions. Highlight key phrases from the manuscript if needed to illustrate points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unbiased and disclose conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Be unbiased and professional. If you feel you might have a conflict of interest, inform the editor that there is a conflict and you should not review this manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume anything about the paper based on perceived author identity; maintain objectivity and disclose any relationships that could bias your review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be polite and diplomatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Be polite and diplomatic. Receiving critical feedback, even when constructive, can be difficult and possibly emotional for the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language similar to what you would use when discussing research at a conference or with your advisor. Unnecessarily harsh wording will reflect badly on you with editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confidential comments for ethical or sensitive issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Most reviews also contain the option to provide confidential comments to the editor, which can be used to provide the editor with more detail on the decision or to raise concerns about plagiarism, data manipulation, or other ethical issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve explicit allegations or unresolved ethical concerns for confidential communication to the editor rather than the public review to authors.
